client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed at my new job in marketing. The deadlines are so tight, and I constantly feel like I’m not measuring up to my coworkers who seem to know exactly what they’re doing. I’m not even sure if therapy can help with this—it feels like the problem is just the job itself.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling quite pressured and unsure in this new role, which can be really draining. When you compare yourself to your coworkers, what kind of thoughts tend to come up for you?

client: I keep thinking that they’re all way more competent than I am and that I’m just faking it until someone figures out I don’t belong there. It’s exhausting to feel like I’m constantly on the verge of being exposed. I don’t know if therapy can really change that—it feels like the problem is just me.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of self-doubt and fear of being “found out,” which can be incredibly draining. Have you noticed any moments, even small ones, where you’ve actually succeeded or felt a bit more confident in your role?

client: There have been a few times where I’ve gotten positive feedback, like when I finished a project ahead of schedule or when my manager said I handled a client call well. But even then, I just think it was luck or that they’re just being nice. It’s hard to take those moments seriously because I’m always waiting for the other shoe to drop.
therapist: It sounds like even when there’s evidence that you’re doing well, it’s hard to let it sink in because the fear of failure feels so strong. What do you think might happen if you allowed yourself to trust those positive moments, even just a little?

client: I guess if I trusted those moments, I’d feel less stressed and maybe even enjoy my job more. But it feels risky—like if I start believing I’m doing okay, I’ll just get complacent and make a huge mistake. I don’t know if I can let my guard down like that.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a real tension between wanting to feel more at ease and the fear that letting your guard down might lead to a mistake. What do you think it would take for you to feel safe enough to trust yourself a bit more in your role?

client: I think it would take a lot less pressure and more time to feel safe trusting myself. But the environment is so fast-paced, and there’s always something new to learn or do. It’s hard to imagine feeling secure when everything feels so high-stakes. Even if I wanted to trust myself, the job itself doesn’t seem to allow for that.
therapist: It sounds like the fast-paced nature of the job is making it really hard to find moments to build confidence, and that can feel like an impossible cycle. What would it look like to take small, manageable steps toward trusting yourself, even in such a high-pressure environment?

client: I guess small steps could mean focusing on one positive moment a day instead of dismissing it. But honestly, it feels like I’d just end up doubting myself again anyway. It’s like my brain automatically goes back to thinking I’m not good enough, no matter what I try. It’s frustrating because I want to feel better, but it’s hard to believe that anything will really change.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught in a cycle where self-doubt keeps pulling you back, even when you try to focus on the positives—and that can feel really discouraging. What would it look like to gently challenge those automatic thoughts, even just a little, when they come up?

client: I guess I could try to ask myself if there’s any evidence that I’m actually failing or if it’s just my fear talking. But it’s hard because the fear feels so real, even if there’s no proof. It’s like my brain is wired to expect the worst, and I don’t know how to unlearn that. It feels like it’s just who I am.
therapist: It sounds like you’re noticing how powerful those fears can feel, even when there’s no real evidence to support them—and that’s a really important insight. What would it feel like to remind yourself, even just once, that fear doesn’t always equal truth?

client: It would feel strange, honestly. Like I’m lying to myself or ignoring something important. Even if fear doesn’t equal truth, it feels so real and convincing that it’s hard to separate it from reality. I don’t know if reminding myself of that would actually change how I feel—it feels like just saying something doesn’t make it true.
therapist: It sounds like reminding yourself that fear isn’t always truth feels almost unnatural, like you’re dismissing something important—and that’s a really honest reflection. What if instead of trying to convince yourself, you simply noticed those fears as thoughts, without needing to fully believe or dismiss them? How might that feel?

client: That might feel a little less overwhelming than trying to convince myself that the fears aren’t real. But I’m not sure how much it would help in the long run—it feels like just noticing them won’t make them go away or stop them from affecting me. I don’t know if that’s enough to change how I feel about my job and my abilities.
therapist: It sounds like you’re open to trying something new, but there’s still some skepticism about whether noticing those fears will make a meaningful difference—and that’s completely understandable. What if noticing them was just the first step, not the solution itself? How might that shift your perspective?

client: I guess if noticing the fears was just the first step, it might feel less overwhelming than trying to fix everything at once. But I’m still not sure what the next steps would be—it feels like noticing them doesn’t really change anything unless I know what to do after that. It’s hard to see how this will actually help me feel better about my job.
therapist: It sounds like you’re willing to take that first step of noticing your fears, but it’s hard to see how that will lead to meaningful change without knowing what comes next—and that uncertainty can feel a bit flat or stuck. What if the next step was simply exploring what happens when you notice those fears, without needing to fix anything right away?
